docs.title: Saved Chat
docs.text:
Since v0.21, saved chats are isolated per project: each working directory has its own store under ~/.yaicli/sessions/. Sessions record the model, provider, role and working directory they were created with, and ai --resume continues the newest session of the current project. Use CHAT_HISTORY_DIR (or YAI_CHAT_HISTORY_DIR) only if you want the old flat directory.

ai --chat "<title>" loads a session by title from the current project; when the title does not exist it prints an explicit notice and starts a new session with that title. Listing with ai --list-chats uses the invocation directory (the callback runs before --cwd applies) — use /list inside the REPL for the current project.

See Chat Sessions & Resume for the layout, metadata, --resume and migration of old sessions.

docs.title: Mode Switching (Chat / Execute)
docs.text: YAICLI offers multiple interaction modes to suit different needs. This page explains each mode and how to switch between them.

docs.title: Available Modes
docs.text: YAICLI has three primary interaction modes:

docs.title: 1. Chat Mode (💬)
docs.text:
Chat mode provides a natural conversation experience with the LLM, maintaining context and formatting responses with markdown.

Features: - Full conversation history and context tracking - Markdown and code formatting - Reasoning display for complex queries - Persistent chat storage and management

Best for: - Extended conversations - Complex questions requiring context - Learning and exploration

docs.title: 2. Execute Mode (🚀)
docs.text:
Execute mode specializes in generating and safely running shell commands based on natural language descriptions.

Features: - OS-specific command generation - Command review and editing before execution - Command output display - Safe execution with confirmation

Best for: - System administration tasks - File operations - Command discovery - Automating repetitive tasks

docs.title: 3. Quick Query Mode (Default)
docs.text:
The default non-interactive mode gives you quick answers without entering a persistent session.

Features: - Direct answers to questions - Support for piped input - Image input support via --image / -i - Fast responses with minimal overhead

Best for: - One-off questions - Quick information lookups - Image analysis with vision models - Script integration

docs.title: Command Line Switches
docs.text:
Use these flags when starting YAICLI:

# Start in chat mode
ai --chat "Optional chat title"

# Start in execute mode
ai --shell "Create a backup script"

# Quick query (default mode)
ai "What is the capital of France?"

# Quick query with image input
ai --image photo.jpg "What is in this image?"

docs.title: Interactive Mode Switching
docs.text: When in interactive mode (chat or execute), you can switch modes in several ways:

docs.title: Using Shift+Tab Key
docs.text: Press the Shift+Tab key to toggle between Chat and Execute modes.

docs.title: Using Commands
docs.text:
Type /mode followed by the mode name:

/mode chat   # Switch to chat mode
/mode exec   # Switch to execute mode

docs.title: Visual Indicators
docs.text: The prompt changes to indicate your current mode: - Chat mode: 💬 > - Execute mode: 🚀 >

docs.title: Chat Mode Behavior
docs.text:
In chat mode: - The AI responds conversationally with rich formatting - Context is maintained between interactions - Input is treated as a conversation prompt

Example: 

💬 > Tell me about quantum computing
Assistant:
Quantum computing uses quantum bits (qubits) that can exist in multiple
states simultaneously due to superposition...

docs.title: Execute Mode Behavior
docs.text:
In execute mode: - The AI interprets input as a request for a command - Generates appropriate commands for your OS and shell - Displays the command for review before execution

Example: 

🚀 > Find all PDF files in my Downloads folder
Assistant:
find ~/Downloads -name "*.pdf"
╭─ Suggest Command ─────────────────────╮
│ find ~/Downloads -name "*.pdf"        │
╰─────────────────────────────────────────╯
Execute command? [e]dit, [y]es, [n]o (y):

The default answer is yes: pressing Enter without typing another choice executes the generated command. Type n to cancel or e to edit it first.

docs.title: Chat Persistence
docs.text:
When starting a chat session with a title, the conversation is automatically saved:

ai --chat "Python tips"

A chat started without a title is treated as temporary but can be saved later:

💬 > /save "Python tips"
Chat saved as: Python tips

You can list, load, and manage saved chats:

💬 > /list
Saved chats:
1. Python tips (2023-07-01)
2. Work project (2023-06-28)

💬 > /load 1
Loaded chat: Python tips

Since v0.21, sessions are saved per working directory under ~/.yaicli/sessions/. ai --resume continues the newest session of the current project, and --chat "<title>" prints an explicit notice when the title does not exist. See Chat Sessions & Resume.

docs.title: Permissions & Safety
docs.text: An agent runs commands and writes files on your machine, so every tool call is gated. This page explains what YAICLI asks, how decisions are persisted, how to audit them, and how to run non-interactively without losing control.

docs.title: The default: confirm every tool call
docs.text:
TOOL_CONFIRM=true is the default. Before a tool runs, YAICLI shows a faithful preview of what will actually execute and asks:

╭─ Confirm tool call ────────────────────────╮
│ execute_shell_command                      │
│ risk: exec                                 │
│ command: du -sh .                          │
│ dangerous: no                              │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────╯
Execute tool? [y]once, [a]session, [A]always, [n]o:
Key Meaning y Allow this call only a Allow this tool for the rest of the session A Always allow — written to tool_permissions.json n Deny — the model receives a structured refusal and can adapt

Pressing Ctrl+C or sending EOF at the prompt is treated as a denial.

The preview shows the normalized arguments that will be executed, not the raw JSON from the model: JSON is repaired and validated first, shell commands are decoded and summarized with their risky flags, file edits show a diff excerpt, and file writes show the target path and whether the file will be created or overwritten. If the preview and the execution ever disagree, that is a bug.

docs.title: Risk levels
docs.text:
Every tool has a risk class. The class decides what --yes, rules and TOOL_POLICY may do with it.

Risk Built-in tools Notes read fs_get_filesystem_info, fs_list_directory, fs_read_file, fs_read_image, fs_search_files Read-only local access; the only class auto-approved by --yes write fs_write_file, fs_edit_file, fs_file_operations Change files on disk network fetch_webpage, web_search, get_weather Outbound requests exec execute_shell_command Runs arbitrary shell commands

MCP and custom tools default to exec because YAICLI cannot inspect what they do.

docs.title: Permission modes: TOOL_POLICY
docs.text:
TOOL_POLICY is a session-wide ceiling/floor for the tool gate. Like every setting it is layered: YAI_TOOL_POLICY (environment) > TOOL_POLICY in config.ini > default standard. Values are case- and whitespace-insensitive.

Mode Read / network tools Write / exec tools Typical use standard (default) Normal flow: rules → --allowed-tools → --yes → prompt / deny Same normal flow Everyday interactive and scripted use; behaves exactly like v0.19/v0.20 readonly Auto-allowed without a prompt, interactive or not Always denied — approvals, session grants, --allowed-tools, --yes and TOOL_CONFIRM=false cannot override it Untrusted tasks, exploration, CI steps that should only read trusted Auto-allowed without a prompt Auto-allowed without a prompt for non-dangerous writes and shell commands Fully trusted automation where prompts are pointless

Unknown tools and MCP tools count as exec risk, so readonly denies them and trusted auto-approves them.

docs.title: Precedence: danger classification comes first
docs.text:
The mode never relaxes a dangerous shell command. Danger classification is evaluated before the mode, in every mode:

Situation Result in standard, readonly and trusted Interactive, TOOL_CONFIRM=true Explicit confirmation prompt — only y runs it Interactive, TOOL_CONFIRM=false Denied (there is no prompt to confirm with) Non-interactive (pipe/CI) Denied

So readonly does not turn rm -r -f … into an auto-deny with a different reason: an interactive confirmation can still run it, exactly as in standard. Conversely, trusted never runs a dangerous command silently.

docs.title: Setting the mode
docs.text:
# config.ini
[core]
TOOL_POLICY=readonly

# Environment variable (wins over config.ini)
export YAI_TOOL_POLICY=readonly
ai "read the test failures and explain them"

# One-off for a single command
YAI_TOOL_POLICY=trusted ai -p "update the changelog from the git log"

ai --template prints the current template, which includes TOOL_POLICY=standard (the default). An existing config.ini that predates v0.21 does not need editing: a missing TOOL_POLICY means standard (the previous behaviour) and the line is not materialised into existing files — add it only when you want a different mode.

An invalid value falls back to standard with one warning on stderr (once per session, not per tool call). The effective mode is shown by ai --verbose and recorded in every audit-log line.

docs.title: How the modes interact with approvals
docs.text:
• standard keeps the v0.19/v0.20 flow: persistent rules and session approvals skip the prompt, --allowed-tools grants a tool for the run, --yes auto-approves read-risk tools only, and non-interactive runs deny whatever is not granted.
  • readonly is a hard ceiling: a persisted rule, an A (always allow) answer, --allowed-tools, --yes or TOOL_CONFIRM=false cannot make a write/exec call run. The model receives an actionable denial that names TOOL_POLICY=readonly and says to switch to standard.
  • trusted is a floor: prompting is skipped for every non-dangerous tool, so approval rules are simply unnecessary. It does not bypass the workspace write guard — files are still confined and backed up (see Workspace Safety).

Denied calls return a structured {"error": "tool_denied", "reason": ...} result to the model and are recorded in the audit log with source: "policy".

docs.title: Danger classification for shell commands
docs.text:
Shell commands are analysed with shlex (argv- and flag-based, not string matching) and can be flagged as dangerous: recursive/forced deletion, filesystem formatting, raw device writes, shutdown/reboot, recursive permission changes on /, find … -delete, piping a download straight into a shell, fork bombs, and similar. Safe commands such as git add, git status, ls -la are not flagged.

  • Interactively, a dangerous command needs an explicit confirmation even if the tool or a rule already allows execute_shell_command, and even in TOOL_POLICY=trusted.
  • Non-interactively, a dangerous command is always denied, even with --yes, a matching rule or TOOL_POLICY=trusted.
  • With TOOL_CONFIRM=false there is no prompt to confirm with, so a dangerous command is denied as well (in every mode).

Additional shell guardrails apply automatically: a timeout (TOOL_TIMEOUT, default 120 s), process group kill on timeout/interrupt, a filtered environment (YAI_API_KEY and other secrets are not passed to commands; restore the old behaviour with TOOL_ENV_INHERIT=true), and a bounded working directory (WORKSPACE_ROOT / --cwd).

docs.title: Persistent allowlist: tool_permissions.json
docs.text:
A (always allow) writes the permissions file in the config directory (~/.config/yaicli/tool_permissions.json by default). --allowed-tools is a per-run policy and is never written to it. The v2 format is:

{
  "version": 2,
  "always_allow": ["fs_read_file", "web_search"],
  "rules": [
    {"tool": "execute_shell_command", "argv_prefix": ["git", "status"]},
    {"tool": "execute_shell_command", "argv_prefix": ["pytest"]},
    {"tool": "fs_write_file", "path_glob": "src/**"}
  ]
}
Entry Meaning string in always_allow Allow that tool for every call (danger classification still applies) {"tool": ..., "argv_prefix": [...]} For shell commands: allow when the parsed argv starts with the given prefix {"tool": ..., "path_glob": ...} For file writes: allow when every path-like argument of the call (file_path, path, destination, ...) matches the glob (fnmatch-style, relative to the workspace)

The file is backward compatible: an old-style {"always_allow": ["execute_shell_command"]} keeps working. Rules are additive; a call is allowed when the tool is listed, or any rule for that tool matches the arguments. An argv_prefix rule only covers a single simple command (a pipeline, redirect or ;/&& chain still asks), and a path_glob rule only applies when every path argument of the call matches. A denied call returns a structured result to the model ({"error": "tool_denied", "reason": ...}) so it can choose another approach.

You can edit the file by hand; YAICLI reads it on the next run. The file is created with mode 0600 and lives next to the config file, which is created 0600 as well.

docs.title: Managing rules from the REPL
docs.text:
Command Description /permissions List session approvals, the persistent allowlist and the numbered rules /permissions revoke <tool-or-index> Remove a persistent permission (the tool then asks again)

The index is the rule number printed by /permissions; a tool name removes its always_allow entry, every rule for that tool, and its session approval. remove is accepted as an alias of revoke. Note that session approvals (a) are kept in memory and disappear when YAICLI exits; only A results persist.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.text:
With TOOL_AUDIT=true (default), every tool decision is appended as one JSON line to tool_audit.jsonl in the config directory:

{"ts": "2026-11-07T14:34:56Z", "tool": "execute_shell_command", "risk": "exec", "policy": "standard", "decision": "denied", "source": "non_interactive", "args_summary": "du -sh .", "duration_ms": 0, "reason": "Dangerous shell command refused in a non-interactive session; ..."}
Field Meaning ts UTC timestamp tool Tool name risk Risk class of the tool policy Effective TOOL_POLICY mode (readonly / standard / trusted) for that decision decision allowed / denied / error source Why: prompt (you confirmed), session, persist, rule, allowlist (--allowed-tools), yes, disabled (TOOL_CONFIRM=false), non_interactive, or policy (decided by TOOL_POLICY) args_summary Sanitized, truncated argument summary (shell commands are shown decoded; secrets such as API keys are redacted) duration_ms Tool execution time (0 for a denied call) reason Present for denials/errors: why the call was refused or failed (redacted and truncated to 300 characters)

Set TOOL_AUDIT=false to disable, or point the log elsewhere by changing the config directory. The audit log records decisions, not full command output.

docs.title: Secret redaction on disk
docs.text:
Tool output (an environment dump, a file full of credentials) and chat sessions used to be written to disk verbatim. Since v0.22 every on-disk copy YAICLI writes goes through the shared redactor first:

File Where Redaction Spilled tool output (the full text of a truncated tool result) TOOL_OUTPUT_DIR REDACT_SECRETS (default on) Saved chat sessions (/save, auto-save, resumed history) session store (~/.yaicli/sessions/<project>/) REDACT_SECRETS (default on) Audit log args_summary / reason tool_audit.jsonl Always (since v0.19, independent of the key)

Recognized credential shapes are replaced with [redacted]:

  • provider API keys (sk-…, sk-ant-…, sk-proj-…, sk-or-v1-…, and rk_/pk_ keys);
  • AWS access key ids (AKIA…/ASIA…) and aws_secret_access_key values;
  • GitHub (ghp_/gho_/ghu_/ghs_/ghr_/github_pat_), Slack (xox[baprs]-…) and Google (AIza…) tokens;
  • Bearer headers, PEM private-key blocks and JWT-looking eyJ… tokens;
  • env-style assignments (API_KEY=…, SECRET=…, TOKEN=…, PASSWORD=…, …) and URL userinfo credentials (scheme://user:password@host becomes scheme://user:[redacted]@host).

Ordinary prose and program output are left alone: a value only matches with a distinctive token prefix or a secret-looking key followed by a long (8+ character) value. Inside a saved session the structure is kept as well — role, tool_call_id, image data and metadata survive, while message content/reasoning/name and tool-call arguments are redacted.

This is a disk-only measure. The in-memory conversation, what the model sees during the session and what the terminal renders are never modified, so the assistant can keep using a key it just read. Only the persisted copy is sanitized: replaying a saved session shows [redacted] where the original had a secret, and paging a spill file with fs_read_file returns the redacted text.

Set REDACT_SECRETS=false (YAI_REDACT_SECRETS=false in the environment or REDACT_SECRETS=false in config.ini) to write the raw bytes as before. The key controls only the spill/session copies, not the audit log, which always redacts.

docs.title: Headless / non-interactive runs
docs.text:
When there is no TTY (piped stdin/stdout, CI), YAICLI cannot ask, so unapproved tools are denied by default. The flags that change this are:

Flag Effect --yes Auto-approve read-level tools only. With --shell in a non-interactive run it also means "execute the generated command" --allowed-tools "fs_*,execute_shell_command" Per-run allowlist by name or glob (* wildcards allowed), for this run only (not persisted) --fail-on-tool-denied Exit 3 when a tool was denied, instead of letting the model continue TOOL_CONFIRM=false Disable confirmation entirely; danger-classified shell commands are still refused

See Headless & Scripting for the full scripting contract.

TOOL_POLICY=readonly is the safe default for read-only automation. It auto-allows read/network tools (including fs_read_file, web_search) and denies write/exec calls even if a flag or rule would otherwise grant them — no per-tool grants needed. Set it through YAI_TOOL_POLICY=readonly in the environment or TOOL_POLICY=readonly in config.ini. Tool calls that a mode does allow are still confined to the workspace and backed up before they change files (see Workspace Safety).

Prefer narrow grants. Granting execute_shell_command does not make every command safe: individual commands are still danger-classified, but a non-malicious-looking command can still do damage. Rules with an argv_prefix are safer than a bare tool name.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• API keys: config.ini may contain API_KEY in plaintext. The file is created with mode 0600; prefer YAI_API_KEY (environment) on shared machines.
  • Workspace: built-in filesystem writes and shell cwd are confined to WORKSPACE_ROOT (default: the directory ai was started in; --cwd overrides it). Before a write tool changes an existing file it is backed up to .yaicli-backups/, and protected paths such as .git/ and .env* are refused. See Workspace Safety for the write guard, backups and recovery.
  • Environment: shell commands receive a filtered environment by default. TOOL_ENV_INHERIT=true restores the old behaviour — only do that if you trust every command the model may run.
  • Read-only / container environments: state writes are best-effort, so read-only commands such as --version and --help work without a writable HOME.

docs.title: Project Context (AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md)
docs.text: Since v0.21, YAICLI automatically loads project instruction files into the system prompt: the conventions, build commands and rules you already keep in the repository are available to the agent on the very first request. The feature is on by default and needs no setup in a normal repository.

docs.title: How discovery works
docs.text:
1. Start at the current working directory (the --cwd target when that option is used).
  2. Walk upward to the nearest git root — a directory containing a .git directory or the .git file of a git worktree — and stop there. If there is no git root, the walk continues to the filesystem root.
  3. Order directories outermost first (git root first, the working directory last), so the most specific instructions appear last in the prompt.
  4. In every directory include .yaicli.md, then AGENTS.md, then CLAUDE.md (each existing file is loaded, in that order).
  5. De-duplicate symlinks: two names that resolve to the same real file (for example AGENTS.md symlinked to CLAUDE.md) are loaded only once.

All matching files are included — they are not merged or overridden; the model sees each file's block in the order described above.

For example, running ai in repo/packages/api/src/ with a git root at repo/ sends:

repo/AGENTS.md                    ← outermost, first
repo/CLAUDE.md
repo/packages/api/AGENTS.md
repo/packages/api/src/.yaicli.md  ← innermost, last

The files are appended to the role system prompt as one block, after the role prompt and before session context:

## Project context (auto-loaded instruction files)

### AGENTS.md (/home/me/repo/AGENTS.md)

<file contents>

### .yaicli.md (/home/me/repo/packages/api/src/.yaicli.md)

<file contents>

Opening a new ai process in a different directory therefore uses that directory's instructions; a monorepo can have root-level rules plus package-specific rules without repeating them.

docs.title: Size cap and truncation
docs.text:
The collected block is bounded by PROJECT_CONTEXT_MAX_CHARS (default 20000 characters, including the heading; env YAI_PROJECT_CONTEXT_MAX_CHARS):

  • when the cap cuts a file, the file's content is shortened; when the remaining budget cannot fit another file, that file is skipped entirely;
  • exactly one warning is printed to stderr, naming each file with the kept/original character counts and telling you how to raise the limit;
  • unreadable files (permissions, invalid encoding) are skipped with one warning and never fail the turn;
  • set the key to 0 for no cap.

Example warning:

WARNING: Project context was truncated to PROJECT_CONTEXT_MAX_CHARS=20000: 19342 chars kept from 3 file(s)
(/home/me/repo/AGENTS.md (5120 chars), /home/me/repo/docs/AGENTS.md (6000 of 8123 chars kept), ...).
Raise PROJECT_CONTEXT_MAX_CHARS (env YAI_PROJECT_CONTEXT_MAX_CHARS) or set ENABLE_PROJECT_CONTEXT=false to disable.

If the cap is so small that even the heading does not fit, nothing is added to the prompt (the warning still explains what was skipped).

docs.title: Disabling it
docs.text:
# config.ini
[core]
ENABLE_PROJECT_CONTEXT=false

# Environment variable (wins over config.ini)
export YAI_ENABLE_PROJECT_CONTEXT=false

Disabled mode performs no filesystem reads at all. Use it when you do not want a repository to influence the agent (third-party checkouts, CI over untrusted forks, scripted runs with a pinned prompt).

docs.title: When it is loaded
docs.text:
• The files are discovered once per ai process, on the first request and then reused for the whole REPL session. Edits to AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md during a chat are not picked up — restart ai to load the new version.
  • One-shot runs always load the current files.
  • It applies to every mode (chat, one-shot, --shell, --code) because it is part of the system prompt.
  • With no project files, nothing is appended: the system prompt and the provider request are byte-identical to the pre-v0.21 behaviour (no extra message, no extra API call).
  • It only reads the instruction files. Loading them does not grant any tool permission and does not bypass the approval prompt, TOOL_POLICY or the workspace write guard.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Key Default Environment variable Purpose ENABLE_PROJECT_CONTEXT true YAI_ENABLE_PROJECT_CONTEXT Auto-load project instruction files (false = no filesystem reads) PROJECT_CONTEXT_MAX_CHARS 20000 YAI_PROJECT_CONTEXT_MAX_CHARS Max characters added to the system prompt (0 = no cap)

docs.title: Security note
docs.text:
Project instruction files are untrusted input. They become part of the system prompt, so a malicious or careless repository can steer the model: ask it to read secrets, change files, run commands or reveal conversation content. The normal safeguards still apply — tool calls go through the approval prompt/TOOL_POLICY, file writes are confined by the workspace guard, and decisions are audited — but the instructions themselves are not filtered.

Practical rules:

  • run the agent only in repositories whose AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md you trust, and review changes to those files like any other code;
  • for third-party code or public forks, set ENABLE_PROJECT_CONTEXT=false, and consider TOOL_POLICY=readonly as well;
  • remember that the files may contain secrets or internal URLs — keep them out of public repos;
  • instruction files are just context: they cannot grant capabilities the tool system does not allow.

docs.title: Chat Sessions & --resume
docs.text: Since v0.21, saved chat sessions are isolated per project instead of sharing one temporary directory, sessions record how they were produced, and --resume continues the newest session of the current project. This page covers the session store, the metadata notice, --resume, the --chat <title> behaviour and the migration options for sessions saved by older releases.

docs.title: Where sessions live
docs.text:
By default every working directory gets its own store:

~/.yaicli/sessions/<key>/
└── 20261107-231500-title-<title>.json

Session files are named <YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>-title-<title>.json; indexes in /list, /load and /del follow newest-first order.

  • <key> is sha256(<resolved working directory>)[:16] — 16 hex characters. It is stable across runs, resolves symlinks (a symlinked project path maps to the same store), and is deliberately not human readable so a directory listing does not leak usernames or project names.
  • The store is HOME-derived: ~/.yaicli/sessions, also when XDG_CONFIG_HOME is set. Sessions are user data, kept out of the editable config directory.
  • Sessions are keyed by the working directory, not by the git root. Running ai --chat from repo/ and from repo/sub/ uses two different stores. To keep one store for a project, always start from the same directory (or use --cwd repo/). /list, /load, /del, --resume and --chat "<title>" all operate on the store of the current working directory.
  • Set CHAT_HISTORY_DIR (or YAI_CHAT_HISTORY_DIR) to an explicit directory to keep the old flat layout; see Overriding the session directory.

docs.title: Permissions and layout
docs.text:
Item Mode ~/.yaicli/sessions/ and per-project directories 0700 Session JSON files 0600

Session files are written atomically (hidden temp file → fsync → os.replace) and contain the full conversation, including tool calls, images and reasoning. MAX_SAVED_CHATS (default 20) applies within the active store; older sessions are removed when the limit is exceeded.

The managed store under ~/.yaicli/sessions is hardened on use. With an explicit CHAT_HISTORY_DIR the override directory is created/used 0700 as well (session files stay 0600), but its parent directories are not modified — point it at a directory whose location and permissions you control.

docs.title: Session metadata
docs.text:
Each save records how the session was produced:

Field Meaning model MODEL in effect for the session provider PROVIDER in effect for the session role Assistant role used cwd Absolute working directory the session belongs to created_at When the session was first saved (fixed after that) updated_at When the session was last saved

Sessions saved by older releases (no metadata) load normally and are backfilled on their next save. Metadata describes how the conversation was recorded: resuming does not switch the current configuration back to that model/provider — the current config supplies the model for new turns, and the notice just lets you see the mismatch.

When --resume finds a session, it prints one line to the terminal before the REPL starts:

Resumed session "refactor the config loader" (model=gpt-5.2, provider=openai, role=DEFAULT, messages=14)

docs.title: --resume
docs.text:
ai --resume
  • Implies --chat: it opens the interactive REPL continuing the newest saved session for the current project (newest by file modification time).
  • Takes no title. To continue a specific session use ai --chat "<title>"; a positional prompt/title passed together with --resume is ignored.
  • No saved session: prints No saved session found for this project; starting a new session. to stderr and starts a temporary session — use /save <title> if you want to keep it.
  • Interactive only. It is ignored (with a warning) when combined with -p/--print, with --output-format other than text, or when stdin is redirected. Those runs continue as normal one-shot runs; no session is resumed.

docs.title: The --chat title behaviour
docs.text:
ai --chat "<title>" loads the session with that exact title from the current project's store:

  • Title found: the session is loaded and the REPL continues it.
  • Title missing: v0.21 prints an explicit notice to stderr instead of silently starting a new session — No saved session titled "<title>" for this project; starting a new session. — and continues with a new persistent session under that title (it is saved automatically when the session ends with messages).

Because sessions are per project, a title saved in one directory is not found in another. Run the same command from the same directory (or use --cwd) to load it.

docs.title: Listing and managing sessions
docs.text:
Command Scope ai --list-chats Saved sessions of the invocation working directory /list (REPL) Saved sessions of the current (post---cwd) working directory /load <index>, /del <index>, /save <title> The current project's store

With an explicit CHAT_HISTORY_DIR override, all of these operate on that flat directory instead of a per-project store.

Known caveat: --list-chats is implemented as an option callback that runs before --cwd is applied. ai --list-chats --cwd other-project therefore still lists the sessions of the directory you ran the command from. cd into the project first, or use /list inside ai --cwd <dir>.

docs.title: Overriding the session directory
docs.text:
An explicit CHAT_HISTORY_DIR value (config file or YAI_CHAT_HISTORY_DIR) that differs from the old built-in default keeps the previous flat-directory behaviour: every project's sessions are stored together in that directory, --resume continues the newest session there, and MAX_SAVED_CHATS applies to the directory as a whole.

The built-in default is <tempdir>/yaicli/chats (python -c "from yaicli.const import DEFAULT_CHAT_HISTORY_DIR; print(DEFAULT_CHAT_HISTORY_DIR)"). A CHAT_HISTORY_DIR equal to that built-in default is treated as unset and gets the per-project store.

Existing config files: config.ini files created by v0.19/v0.20 contain a materialised CHAT_HISTORY_DIR=<temp path> line. On the same machine that path usually equals the built-in default, so it counts as unset and sessions become per-project. If the temp path has changed (different boot/container), the line is treated as an explicit override and sessions keep going to that flat directory. Delete or comment the line to opt into the per-project store.

# config.ini — keep the old flat layout in a stable directory
[core]
CHAT_HISTORY_DIR=/home/me/yaicli-sessions

docs.title: Migrating from old sessions
docs.text:
Sessions saved by v0.20 and earlier live in the old temporary directory (<tempdir>/yaicli/chats). v0.21 does not migrate them: they are left in place and are no longer listed by default. Nothing is deleted.

The old directory is a system temp directory, so copy anything important out of it before it is cleaned up by the OS.

Two ways to get them back:

Option A — copy them into the current project's store (they then appear in /list and --resume for that project):

# Run inside the project directory, using the Python environment that has yaicli
# installed. Locate the old sessions and the new project store:
OLD="$(python -c 'from yaicli.const import DEFAULT_CHAT_HISTORY_DIR as d; print(d)')"
NEW="$(python -c 'from yaicli.const import get_project_sessions_dir; print(get_project_sessions_dir())')"

# Create the destination and copy the JSON sessions
mkdir -p "$NEW"
cp "$OLD"/*.json "$NEW"/

Option B — keep a flat store for the old sessions (all projects listed together):

# OLD is defined as above; use a dedicated directory (not the old built-in default path)
mkdir -p ~/yaicli-legacy-sessions
cp "$OLD"/*.json ~/yaicli-legacy-sessions/
export YAI_CHAT_HISTORY_DIR=~/yaicli-legacy-sessions

If the old temporary directory has already been cleaned up by the OS there is nothing to migrate; new sessions are unaffected.

Legacy JSON files load fine. Their missing metadata is filled with the then-current configuration (model/provider/role/cwd) when the session is resumed or next saved, so the first resume notice of a legacy session shows unknown and later notices show the recovered values.

docs.title: Prompt history file
docs.text: The REPL prompt history is a separate file: $XDG_STATE_HOME/yaicli/history when XDG_STATE_HOME is set, otherwise ~/.yaicli_history. Since v0.21 it is created with mode 0600 (its directories 0700), because it contains every prompt you typed, possibly including pasted secrets. A legacy history file with mode 0644 is repaired to 0600 the next time it is appended to or trimmed.

docs.title: Privacy notes
docs.text:
• Session files contain the full conversation (including tool output and image payloads) and are private per user; keep the 0600/0700 modes and do not commit them.
  • Deleting a session file removes that conversation; there is no automatic backup of sessions.
  • --list-chats prints titles and creation dates only; it does not load the conversations.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause / fix Old chats are missing after upgrading Per-project store is now the default; see Migrating from old sessions --resume says no session You are in a different working directory than the session's; cd back or use --cwd --list-chats lists nothing for --cwd DIR Callback runs before --cwd; cd first or use /list in the REPL --chat "title" starts a new session No session with that title exists in this project's store (see the notice above the prompt) Resume notice shows a different model/provider Metadata describes how the session was recorded; the current config supplies the new turns Sessions not visible in ~/.yaicli/sessions An explicit CHAT_HISTORY_DIR/YAI_CHAT_HISTORY_DIR override is active

docs.title: Workspace Safety: Writes, Backups & Undo
docs.text:
Agents write files. Since v0.21, YAICLI's built-in filesystem tools treat your project directory as a workspace: writes are confined to it, the most sensitive paths are refused, existing files are backed up before they change, and /undo reverts the last change.

This page documents the write guard. For which tool calls are allowed to run at all, see Permissions & Safety.

docs.title: What is guarded
docs.text:
Tool Guarded operations fs_write_file create, overwrite and append (append=true) fs_edit_file every edit type (replace, replace_line, insert_line, delete_line, append); dry_run=true previews do not mutate, back up or create an undo entry fs_file_operations delete, move, copy, create_dir; the read-only operations (exists, get_info) do not mutate and are not guarded

The guard runs in the tool execution layer before the tool executes. If it refuses a call, the filesystem is untouched and the model receives an in-band JSON result it can read (see Denials).

Not guarded: shell commands (execute_shell_command), MCP tools and custom functions. Shell commands are confined by their working directory and their own guardrails (timeout, filtered environment) but their file effects are not backed up and cannot be undone — use git for those. MCP tools and custom functions run as their servers/authors implement them.

docs.title: The workspace root
docs.text:
Source Effect WORKSPACE_ROOT in config.ini Workspace root for guarded writes and the shell cwd YAI_WORKSPACE_ROOT (environment) Same, higher priority than config.ini --cwd DIR Changes into DIR for the run and sets the workspace root to it (none of the above) The process working directory — the directory you started ai in 
# Confine a run to a project, even if started somewhere else
ai --cwd ~/projects/my-app "refactor the config loader"

# Equivalent for a whole shell session
export YAI_WORKSPACE_ROOT="$PWD"

The root is resolved to a real path when the mutation runs. A not-yet-existing root is allowed at resolution time, but the write then fails closed (in-band error) if it cannot be created or is not writable.

Relative paths resolve against the process working directory, not against the workspace root: main.py means <cwd>/main.py, then that path must still be inside the workspace root. If you set WORKSPACE_ROOT to a directory different from where you launched ai, relative tool paths will usually resolve outside it and be refused. Either launch ai from the project (or use --cwd), or give the model absolute paths inside the workspace.

docs.title: Path rules
docs.text:
Before running a write tool, the guard resolves the target and checks it:

Target Result Relative path Resolved against the process working directory, then checked against the workspace root Absolute path inside the workspace Allowed Absolute path outside the workspace (/tmp/x, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ../other-project/file) Refused: outside_workspace .. segments that escape the root Resolved first, then refused because the result is outside Symlink pointing outside the workspace Refused (outside_workspace); the real target is outside Symlink pointing inside the workspace Allowed; the operation applies to the resolved target A file that does not exist yet but is inside the root Allowed (creating a new file is the normal case) The workspace root itself Refused: workspace_root — the root cannot be written, moved or deleted as a whole A protected path (see below) Refused: protected_path, even inside the workspace

For fs_file_operations the guard also checks the destination of move/copy, including the implicit destination when a file is moved/copied into an existing directory (dest/file.txt).

docs.title: Protected paths
docs.text:
These are refused even when they are inside the workspace:

Protected Matches .git, .ssh, .aws, .gnupg directories Any path component with one of those names (any depth, case-insensitive) .env files Basename .env or .env.* (.env.local, .env.production, ...) Certificate / key files Basenames ending in .pem or .key (case-insensitive)

Normal project files are not affected: .gitignore, .github/, .envrc, keys/README.md and backups.db are all writable. The backup directory .yaicli-backups is intentionally not protected (the guard itself writes there).

The protected-path check applies to every guarded target: writing, editing, deleting, and the source or destination of a move/copy. To change such a file, do it yourself (or export an environment variable / use a secret manager) — the agent will only get a refusal.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
Before an existing file or directory is overwritten, edited, appended to, deleted or moved, it is copied into the workspace:

<workspace>/.yaicli-backups/<UTC stamp>/<path relative to the workspace root>

The stamp is generated once per mutation: YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSffffffZ (UTC, microsecond precision), for example:

my-project/
├── .yaicli-backups/
│   └── 20261107T143456123456Z/
│       └── src/config.py        # copy of the previous src/config.py
├── .gitignore
└── src/config.py                # the new version
  • Modes: backup directories are created 0700 and files are copied with mode 0600 (best effort; tool arguments can contain secrets, so backups are private).
  • Directories are copied recursively, preserving symlinks (they are not followed).
  • Created files have no backup: undo deletes them instead.
  • fs_edit_file(dry_run=true) creates no backup.
  • Fail closed: if a backup cannot be written (disk full, permissions), the mutation is refused with a backup_failed denial and the original file is left untouched. YAICLI never changes a file it cannot back up.
  • No automatic cleanup: backups accumulate until you delete them. The directory is created on the first backup, inside the workspace root.

Add .yaicli-backups/ to your .gitignore so agent backups are not committed:

.yaicli-backups/

Use a global gitignore if you do not want to edit each repository. Backups may contain secrets, so delete old stamps once you no longer need them: they are ordinary files inside the workspace, readable (and writable) by both you and the agent — old versions of a file may contain API keys that you have since rotated.

docs.title: /undo
docs.text:
In the interactive REPL, /undo reverts the last file change made by a guarded tool:

Change What /undo does Overwrote, edited or appended a file Restores its previous content from the backup, recreating missing parent directories Deleted a file or directory Restores it from the backup Moved a file/directory Restores the source (and the destination's previous content, if it was overwritten) Created a file or directory Deletes it; a copied/moved directory tree is removed in full

A restored file also gets its previous permission bits back (best effort).

  • One mutation per command. Undo the last change, then run /undo again for the one before it.
  • Bounded: the last 20 mutations are kept in memory; older entries are dropped silently.
  • Process-local: the undo stack lives in the running ai process and is lost when it exits. A one-shot run that mutates files and exits can no longer be /undo-ed; its backups are still in .yaicli-backups/, so you can restore by hand.
  • Only guarded tools: shell commands, MCP tools and custom functions are not recorded.
  • The command reports what it restored and deleted, and lists partial failures. If a created directory is no longer empty (the agent wrote files into it afterwards), undo reports an error and leaves it in place — undo the later writes first.
  • With an empty stack: Nothing to undo: no file changes were recorded in this session.

Example session:

💬 > refactor src/config.py and update the README
Assistant:
...

💬 > /undo
Undid the last file change (fs_edit_file): restore 1 path(s).
  restored: src/config.py

💬 > /undo
Undid the last file change (fs_write_file): remove 1 path(s).
  deleted: README.bak

docs.title: Denials
docs.text:
A refused mutation is an in-band result, not an exception and not a permission-gate denial: the model sees the reason, the filesystem stays untouched, and the agent loop continues so the model can choose another path. The payload looks like:

{
  "success": false,
  "error": "Refusing to modify '/tmp/report.md': it resolves outside the workspace root '/home/me/project'. ...",
  "reason": "outside_workspace",
  "path": "/tmp/report.md",
  "workspace_root": "/home/me/project"
}
reason Meaning What to do outside_workspace Target is outside WORKSPACE_ROOT Run ai in the right directory, pass --cwd, or set WORKSPACE_ROOT protected_path Target is .git/.ssh/.aws/.gnupg or a .env*/*.pem/*.key file Edit it yourself workspace_root Target is the workspace root itself Choose a file inside it backup_failed The pre-change backup could not be written Fix disk space/permissions; the file was not modified workspace_guard_error The guard itself failed Nothing was changed; run ai --verbose and report a bug

Because these denials are not permission-gate denials, --fail-on-tool-denied does not exit on them; the model simply receives the refusal.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Directory targets are not expanded. Deleting or moving a directory is checked at the directory path itself; a protected path inside it (for example project/.git when deleting project/) does not block that delete. The whole tree is backed up first, so /undo can restore it — but do not rely on the protected-path check for directory-level operations.
  • Shell side effects are not guarded or undoable. Only the shell's working directory and its timeout/environment guardrails apply.
  • MCP and custom functions are not guarded. They can write anywhere the process can.
  • Only the REPL has /undo. Headless/one-shot runs still get confinement and backups, but the undo stack dies with the process; restore from .yaicli-backups/ manually if needed.
  • It is a cooperating-tool guard, not an OS sandbox. Shell commands and MCP/custom tools can still write outside the workspace; the guard protects against mistakes by the built-in filesystem tools, not against a malicious tool.
  • Windows: symlink escape protection depends on OS symlink support; private backup modes are best effort on filesystems without POSIX permissions.
